I am 78 years old and have farmed my land in Quzhou County for more than 50 years. My wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October, and now in early spring it is greening up. I have 5 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I will stick with what I know: winter wheat followed by summer maize. Everyone in my village does this rotation, and at my age I cannot afford to take risks with new crops. My son helps me hire the rotary tiller for wheat planting and the combine for harvest, but I make all the decisions myself.

For my wheat, I will topdress with urea around jointing stage and irrigate three times — once now in spring, once at heading, and once at grain filling. Water from the well costs money, but wheat needs it. I use about 100 jin of compound fertilizer as basal and another 50 jin of urea topdressing, which works out to roughly 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus the phosphorus and potassium from the compound. I spray insecticide twice and herbicide once, and usually fungicide once if the weather turns humid. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the weather cooperates — that is what I have gotten in most years.

For summer maize, I will plant right after wheat harvest in early June. There is no time for tillage — we always no-till plant maize into the wheat stubble. I buy hybrid seed every year, usually Nongda or Denghai varieties, because saved maize seed does not breed true. I put down about 80 jin of compound fertilizer at planting, which gives me around 12 kg nitrogen per mu. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat. I irrigate twice and spray for pests and weeds three times total. If the summer rains are normal, I expect about 550 kg per mu.

I would like to apply more fertilizer, but I am cash-constrained and at my age I prefer stability. This plan is enough to feed my family and sell a little grain.
